Date: April 1, 1955 From: Laboratory Docent N. Ivanov To: Senior Genetic Engineer A. Raguzin  Please read this carefully. It is not a joke! Yesterday, while disposing of organic waste, I deposited several carcasses of pigs that had expired during experiments into the Sprout-breeding chamber. We checked the recordings again today to see where the Vovas have been going, and I discovered that the pigs had gotten up, walked around the chamber, and even tried to get outside. Unfortunately, by the time I got there, the carcasses had been eaten. There may be something we don't know about the Sprouts. I insist that we study this incident.

Date: April 1, 1955 From: Junior Genetic Engineer E. Malakhova To: Senior Genetic Engineer A. Raguzin  Vavilov pulled the plug on my project! He said it was "illogical" and "favored form over substance." Can you believe that?! If we can make Sprouts, why do we have to breed regular cold-resistant or heat-resistant plants? If we want to settle new worlds, maybe we should create new plants there. Look, I love our Russian birch forests, but if I fly to, say, Cuba, I want to see palm trees and reeds. You know, something new! We shouldn't grow fucking apple trees on Mars, we should grow flaming Martian beehive cacti, or stalks of electric wheat! We've got the chance to make a new world unlike any other, and we're growing cabbage! Gimme a break...

Date: June 1, 1955 From: VDNH Press Secretary M. Gabriashvili To: #VDNH_staff  Dear comrades, immediately following universal polymerization, we will begin building a new campus that will be completely dedicated to flying machines and the triumph of Soviet aircraft. The complex will be erected in the air directly above the VDNH, and visitors will be transported to it via a new technology called airevators. In connection with this, a new contest has been announced: employees are invited to submit ideas for the new entryway. The core concepts that should be reflected include: loftiness, freedom, the blue sky, the triumph of science, and reaching for the stars.  Submissions will be accepted until the end of June 15. Winners will receive a prize and a place on the board of honor.

Date: June 1, 1955 From: Museum Manager M. Yelizarova To: Burav room terminal  Please remember this when giving tours:  The Burav is the crown jewel of Soviet heavy industry and the pride of the Facility. When talking about it, don't forget to mention the following facts:  - The device saves about 10,000 man hours per month  - One large Burav costs as much as a rocket ship  - The technology used to manufacture the device is so complex, the slightest miscalculation can render it unusable - A Burav can reach a depth equal to that of the Mariana Trench after just two weeks of continuous operation - Burav technology was inspired by the inventor Trebelov's design for an underground ship - Burav prototypes were used as combat units in the war, delivering powerful explosives behind enemy lines. They were given the code name "Zmei Gorynich" (a dragon from Slavic mythology) - Smaller Buravs, which their builders affectionately refer to as "bravvies," work beneath us day and night, expanding the Facility's underground space (I'm not 100% sure about this last one—maybe we shouldn't tell visitors about the underground buildings)

Date: May 1, 1955 From: Mechanization Specialist T. Kopylova To: Inventory Manager K. Osenev  It is my duty to bring to your attention that Comrade Kislevsky, who is responsible for stockpiling lumber, has taken several Laborer robots into his possession and put them in his chicken coop. When asked "why?', Comrade Kislevsky responded that he loves raising chickens and wants to create the impression that he has domestic fowl. He claims that the robots resemble rutting roosters. Please do something about this. It's bad enough that he stole registered devices; it also looks unbelievably stupid!

Date: June 1, 1955 From: Museum Manager M. Yelizarova To: Burav room terminal  Tour guides, please take note:  Remember that, unlike other devices manufactured at the Facility, Buravs are not sent abroad. But don't focus on this, and try to avoid related topics if you can.  By the same token, watch visitors very carefully and don't let them examine the device too closely or for too long. Photography is strictly prohibited.  When dealing with a foreign delegation, distract them with a game, show them slides of projects completed by Buravs, and make sure you don't give them time to examine the device directly. Do not provide direct answers to questions of a technical nature.

Date: June 2, 1955 From: Facility 3826 Deputy Director M. Stockhausen To: Museum Manager M. Yelizarova  I got a call from the general secretary's office in Moscow yesterday. A group of college students are taking a trip here, but they're no ordinary students—they're the children of very important people. I want you to give them a tour personally, Comrade Yelizarova. And, before you object, I will tell you right now that this is not a matter for discussion.  The children must be given a tour of the entire museum. They must be shown everything, and they must be impressed. Show them everything and make sure they don't get bored.

Date: June 2, 1955 From: Junior Exhibit Curator M. Kalinina To: #tour_guides  "Transformer rooms represent the next step in the development of Soviet housing and industry. Our promising designs for mobile buildings take all necessary requirements into account, from wind resistance and earthquake stability to residents' need to relax and work in comfort. Dreadful holdovers from the era of capitalism such as communal apartments, workers' barracks, and other "human ant hills" inherited by the Soviet Union from the failed Tsarist state will soon be a thing of the past." Note for tour guides: the exhibit pieces are currently undergoing maintenance, so visitors are allowed to look at the transforming rooms, but can't enter them. Failure to comply could lead to injury, or even death.

Date: June 2, 1955 From: VDNH Security Manager K. Ismailov To: #tour_guides  It's no secret that our employees have an ambivalent attitude to the VDNH. Some of you think it's just a museum full of exhibits, but I'd like to remind you that the VDNH is where our visitors first encounter our innovations, so just as much watchfulness and caution is required here as at Vavilov or Pavlov's secret labs. Foreign tourists regularly try to get into work areas and touch the exhibits. I'm not saying that we need to treat them all like spies, but keep in mind that every visitor is a potential enemy agent. Don't let your guard down!

Date: April 3, 1955 From: Vavilov Complex Manager S. Vavilov To: #cold_workshop  Dear comrades, I'd like to call your attention to the fact that our work has borne fruit—literally! Our experiments related to growing seeds in lunar soil in conditions approaching a hypothetical lunar greenhouse have been a stunning success. Unfortunately, given the importance and great promise of this work, we still can't share our results, even with the members of the team, but you will all learn about the contribution you have made to science very soon. Thank you again for laboring for the future of humanity, comrades.

Date: April 3, 1955 From: Security Manager V. Nyukhov To: #security_employees  I'd like to call your attention to the fact that Zinaida Muravyova, AKA Granny Zina, is not allowed to enter or approach the sapling warehouse without authorization under any circumstances. Comrade Muravyova has previously taken seeds and saplings of experimental flowers back to her dwelling under the pretext of performing an inspection, then cultivated them privately. Since these plants are in early experimental stages and may have characteristics that have yet to be fully studied, this could be dangerous.  P.S. Don't react to Granny Zina's rudeness. Behave yourselves.

Date: April 3, 1955 From: Vavilov Complex Manager S. Vavilov To: Vavilov Complex Assistant Manager V. Zolotukhin  Urgent! All the results of our experiments cultivating seeds in lunar soil are to be made secret, and all samples except for one are to be destroyed. Discussing or documenting what grew from the seeds during the experiment is prohibited. Isolated samples are to receive Red 3 status and be transported to the Academy of Consequences in a sealed Polymer container. Come up with a plausible story about the results for employees.  P.S. We will most likely have to think long and hard about what we really know about our satellite.

Date: April 4, 1955 From: #visitor2743 To: review_book  Dear managers, I'm a war veteran, Major Viktor Rukh. I've been wanting to come to your museum for a long time now. But now that I've been here, I'm disappointed. Where's the military tech? Our military machines are famous all over the world, so why can't I see them during peacetime? Your robot helpers are interesting, of course. But I want to see Mastiffs, Unicorns, and all the other amazing stuff that saved our butts in WWII! I hope you can fix this real soon.

Date: June 8, 1955 From: M. Styzhev, secretary to Comrade Pavlov to: Pavlov Cultural Archivist V. Nikitin  Vitaly, you know that Comrade Pavlov has been a little anxious lately, and I am aware that he keeps sending you requests for archival data on various projects from Pavlov, especially on the threshold of the launch of Kollektiv 2.0. So I've got a little request for you. Comrade Pavlov is, shall we say, getting on in years. We should try to keep his worries to a minimum. He's a talented scientist, but he's become painfully sentimental in recent years. If you get any requests regarding particularly complex issues, just stall him for a bit and tell me right away.  I'll make it worth your while.

Date: June 9, 1955 From: Inventory Manager K. Osenev To: Watchman E. Puodjunas  I'll tell you one more time: robots don't get tired and have no physical or psychological need for rest. Your request for leave for them is denied.  Seriously, Yegor, I get that you're an older person who was born back in the 19th century. But would you give a tractor or a sewing machine a vacation? I know the robots act like people, but they're just tools, like a wrench or a car. And they're created to make our lives easier, not the other way around.

Date: June 4, 1955 From: E. Puojunas To: Inventory Manager K. Osenev  Comrade Osenev, the robots are working all day long and I bet they're really tired. Let's give them a break, okay? Are they galley slaves or something?! All of us we can help them do their work, and they can relax and take a break which they never do. It pains me to see it, you know. We could do it easy since we're working people and we're used to it!

Date: May 4, 1955 From: Museum Manager M. Yelizarova To: all_managers  Due to the direct conflict between S. Lastochkin, the manager of Plisetskaya Theater, and our management staff, VDNH employees will no longer be given theater tickets as incentives.  We cannot tolerate their behavior, comrades. Everyone knows that the theater has become a den of iniquity under that pompous dandy's leadership. I frequently receive messages about what's happening backstage. Shield yourself and your subordinates from these bourgeois vices unworthy of a Soviet citizen!

Date: May 4, 1955 From: Tour Guide L. Liteikina To: Museum Manager M. Yelizarova   The VDNH security manager has used his clout to make his old army buddy M. Gabriashvili press secretary. I would like to emphasize that said army buddy has no education to speak of, and not only has he never worked at a museum before, he's never even set foot in one (his own words). I realize that he's an officer and a war veteran, but a man with no knowledge of the field does not belong in this position. Please look into it.

Date: June 5, 1955 From: VDNH Security Manager K. Ismailov To: Senior Engineer V. Martashev  Vlad, I've heard that the Beluga hanging in the exhibit room is fully equipped and even has a working engine. Can you imagine what would happen if someone presses the wrong button on that thing? Best-case scenario, it'd knock down walls... and I don't even want to think about the worst-case scenario. Remove the motor and put up barriers right away, or I'll send you to Vavilov!

Date: June 5, 1955 From: Visitation Dept. Manager K. Loginova To: VDNH Security Manager K. Ismailov  It is my duty to inform you that S. Lastochkin, the director of Plisetskaya Theater, has adopted the habit of inviting his guests, who frequently leave his institution in a less-than-sober state, to the VDNH. These loud, tipsy visitors have been behaving in an unacceptable fashion. However, since they are often high-ranking officials, there is no way to control them. Please find a way to prevent Lastochkin's guests from entering the museum.

Date: June 5, 1955 From: Service Settlement Manager I. Abdurakhimov To: Club President P. Savelyeva  Next Monday, June 13, 1955, the triumphant launch of Kollektiv 2.0 will take place. However, due to the work schedules of employees residing in the village, not everyone will be able to go to the VDNH. So please celebrate where you are. Here is the schedule:  1:00 PM: Work day ends  1:00-2:00 PM: Lunch  2:00 PM: Gather in the auditorium/town square/foyer  3:00 PM: Speeches by senior managers, celebration, broadcasts of speeches by Facility managers  4:30 PM: Launch of Kollektiv 2.0  6:00 PM: Celebratory dinner (cafeteria/foyer)

Date: June 5, 1955 From: Service Settlement Manager I. Abdurakhimov To: Watchman E. Puojunas  Comrade Puojunas, the incidents of supplies disappearing or being stolen have increased. We still haven't told the higher-ups about it yet, but I need you to be more watchful. I've heard you were a Red Commissar during the revolution, so do a me a favor and catch those crooks before we get our asses handed to us on a platter.

Date: March 6, 1955 From: Office Manager A. Vybegallo To: K. Sherman, Design Dept. I have nothing but respect for the Czech furniture factory, but I've got a great idea: let's use Vavilov's facilities to make our own. We've been getting a lot of prisoners lately, an they're all reasonably competent. Plus, they're always recycling all kinds of pine trees and birch trees that didn't pass inspection, stuff like that. As office manager, it pains me to see this. Maybe it just seems like excess lumber to you scientists, but to me, it's wasted potential.  We could supply the whole Facility with its own furniture made from unique species. It's a great idea, n'est-ce pas? Plus, every set of furniture would be what the French call "la exclusif!"
